Who Should Own the Expert Cache? Kernel-Managed Tiering for Trillion-Parameter MoE Inference

Yuan Si Affiliation: University of Waterloo, Waterloo, Canada , Yufeng Lin Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Macau, China , Daming Li Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Mountain View, USA and Jialu Zhang Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: University of Waterloo, Waterloo, Canada
Abstract.

Mixture-of-experts models whose expert pools exceed DRAM capacity require a weight-residency tier. Existing systems manage it in user space with expert-granular placement, frequency-based admission, and explicit pinning. We evaluate whether the operating system page cache can instead serve as the expert tier, using router traces from three MoE models with 128 to 896 experts per layer; the trillion-parameter production model’s traces are replayed natively against its full 1.45 TB expert pool on GH200 hardware. Capacity is enforced by three independent mechanisms.

Iteration time varies smoothly with cache size (run-to-run spread ≤4%\leq 4\%), and device traffic follows the same trend. Under severe pressure the outcome depends on reclaim: device traffic rises above miss demand only when MGLRU, the tested kernels’ default, is combined with balloon-style, mostly mlocked memory, a result reproduced on two machines; cgroup limits and mem= boots show no such behavior, so balloon-based studies can overstate low-capacity device traffic by about 2×2\times. At equal enforced memory, kernel recency serves essentially the same demand as an oracle static-frequency policy computed from the replay trace. In the pread-based replay the oracle-pinned arena stays 1.09–1.11×\times faster—a gap that is the cost of the page-cache hit and reclaim path—but its static table degrades under domain shift while recency remains stable. At 64.7% measured recall, router lookahead changes median time by 0.3% when delivered as kernel readahead advice; perfect one-layer advice gains 5.0% through the same interface and nothing through blocking reads. End-to-end at ample capacity, enabling page-cache admission speeds steady decode by 1.09–1.10×\times in a production CUDA engine with token-identical outputs. These measurements favor kernel-managed eviction, with model knowledge applied to admission and predictive advice.

1. Introduction

A trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model routes every token through a small, input-dependent subset of its weights. In the production model studied here, an accepted token requires on average 1585 expert reads of 17.55 MB each, or 27.8 GB drawn from a 1.45 TB pool. No single node holds that pool in DRAM, so serving systems in this regime require a weight-residency tier. Existing MoE serving systems typically manage expert residency in user space using activation statistics, explicit pinning, prefetching, and CPU/GPU or storage offload (Xue et al., 2025; Rajbhandari et al., 2022; Eliseev and Mazur, 2023; Du et al., 2024; Hwang et al., 2024; Kamahori et al., 2025). The production engine instrumented in this study bypasses the page cache entirely (§2).

We evaluate an alternative design: map the expert pool, read it through the zero-copy path of a companion study (Si et al., 2026), and let the kernel page cache manage host-memory residency. We capture router traces from three MoE models spanning 128 to 896 experts per layer. The production model’s traces are replayed natively against the full 1.45 TB pool on a GH200 node; the other two models drive the fair-window policy simulations of §3, and Qwen3-30B-A3B is additionally replayed on Darwin (§4). The capacity sweep uses three randomized runs per point, and the equal-memory comparison two interleaved repetitions; every replay campaign uses block-layer I/O measurement and capacity control through a balloon, a cgroup wall, or a physical mem= boot. When reclaim policy is held fixed, at least two capacity mechanisms give consistent results for the capacity sweep of §4. The equal-memory and prefetch experiments (§6, §7) use the cgroup wall, and §5 analyzes the one configuration in which the mechanisms disagree. The static-frequency baseline is given oracle access to the trace being replayed, which makes the comparison favorable to that policy.

  • •

    Capacity is a smooth, measurable parameter. Iteration time varies smoothly with cache size (run-to-run spread ≤\leq4%), and measured device traffic follows the same monotone trend. A demand model without fitted bandwidth constants compares simulated misses with block-layer device counters and identifies re-read amplification at each capacity (§4).

  • •

    Low-capacity amplification depends on reclaim configuration. Low-capacity amplification requires both MGLRU and a balloon-style host with a high fraction of mlocked memory. It appears in the balloon at 81% locked memory (C=64C{=}64 GB) and not at 74% (C≈93C{\approx}93 GB); the non-balloon cells—the cgroup wall at C=64C{=}64 GB and the physical mem= boot at ≈93{\approx}93 GB—show no amplification. The result is reproduced on two machines and shows that balloon-based sizing experiments can overstate low-capacity device traffic by approximately 2×2\times (§5).

  • •

    Recency is effective at host-tier capacities. Under identical evaluation windows, LRU matches or exceeds the same-domain oracle static-frequency table from B=32B{=}32 experts per layer upward, which covers every host-memory budget evaluated here. At trillion scale it reaches approximately 70% of Belady’s optimum. At the smallest simulated budget (B=8B{=}8), frequency performs better because LRU cannot retain the immediate reuse set. Under domain shift, the static table falls to 21–45% while LRU remains at 70–71%; global and per-layer allocation differ by at most 2.7 pp (§3, §6).

  • •

    Pinned ownership retains a bounded mechanism advantage. Under an enforced equal-memory limit with verified mlock state and warm pages charged to the same budget, the oracle-pinned arena is 1.09–1.11×\times faster than the page cache in the pread-based replay, with nearly identical device traffic. The device counters rule out byte selection as the cause; the residual cost lies in the page-cache hit and reclaim path (§6).

  • •

    Delivery semantics limit the value of prediction. The router predictor’s recorded plan, replayed at 64.7% measured recall, changes median time by 0.3% when delivered through fadvise, and yields no measurable benefit through synchronous prefetch. Perfect one-layer advice gains 5.0% through the same advisory interface and nothing through blocking reads. Belady bounds the remaining miss-reduction potential at roughly one third of the misses LRU still incurs (§7).

  • •

    Measured constants give the placement rules. Admission follows from the miss already incurred, and the promotion threshold from measured bandwidths, with no fitted parameters. In a production engine at ample capacity, enabling page-cache admission improves steady decode by 1.09–1.10×\times with token-identical outputs (§8, §9).

2. Background and the Incumbent Design

The workload.

A decoder-only MoE layer routes each token to kk of EE experts. The production model studied here uses k=16k{=}16 and E=896E{=}896 across 92 routed layers, for 82,43282{,}432 experts totaling 1.45 TB at int4; its dense “spine” (attention, shared projections, and routers) occupies a further 114 GB (Kimi Team, 2026). During decode, the spine is read at every step while the routed subset changes. The resulting expert traffic—1663 expert reads, 29.2 GB per engine iteration—is the workload studied in this paper. Two open models extend the expert-count range: Qwen3-30B-A3B (k=8k{=}8, E=128E{=}128, 48 layers, 17.6 GB) and DeepSeek-V3 (k=8k{=}8, E=256E{=}256, 58 routed layers of 61) (Qwen Team, 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2024). Assumptions that hold at 128 experts per layer no longer hold at 896; the observed transition lies between 128 and 256 (§3).

The incumbent design.

Systems for larger-than-memory MoE inference commonly manage expert residency explicitly in user space, using activation statistics, prefetching, pinning, and CPU/GPU or storage offload (Xue et al., 2025; Rajbhandari et al., 2022; Eliseev and Mazur, 2023; Du et al., 2024; Hwang et al., 2024; Kamahori et al., 2025; Yi et al., 2025). This design entails three testable assumptions: expert popularity is stable enough to guide placement (§3), the expert is an appropriate allocation granularity (§6), and admitting expert pages to the OS cache would be counterproductive (§6, §9). The production engine used for the traces applies the third assumption throughout: F_NOCACHE on every expert read.

Capturing routing.

Routing is captured through a trace hook in the production engine and a 40-line evaluation callback in llama.cpp. The protocol records only decode, because batched prefill mixes positions and llama.cpp’s scheduler dry run emits a synthetic first pass, identifiable from bit-identical “step 0” coverage across four prompts. Replay uses the same per-expert files read by the engine, so the replayed I/O stream corresponds directly to engine I/O.

What capacity denotes.

We keep six quantities distinct: the target provided to a capacity mechanism (“capacity CC”); MemAvailable; resident file-backed pages; locked anonymous pages (VmLck); block-device reads from /proc/diskstats sectors, which measure block-layer request bytes rather than physical-media bytes; and logical expert accesses from the trace. Three independent mechanisms enforce CC: a balloon, a cgroup-v2 MemoryMax wall, and a boot-time mem= limit. The mechanisms agree except under the reclaim configuration analyzed in §5. Every run records MemAvailable, Cached, Mlocked, and Unevictable at the start of the measured loop, together with the cgroup peak when applicable.

A canonical trace parser.

Speculative decoding makes “one token” an ambiguous accounting unit. An engine iteration may contain two positions, represented by a 32-index record when speculation succeeds, or may route one layer twice when a failed speculation is followed by a fallback pass. Collapsing these cases biases downstream denominators. Because the trace JSONL has no explicit event tag, the canonical parser reconstructs each record as normal, spec-accept, or spec-fallback from record width and per-layer duplication. Across all four domains, the typed accounting recovers exactly 299 accepted tokens per trace for an engine request of 300. Replay timing is reported in engine iterations and serving arithmetic in accepted tokens. All subsequent analyses use this typed parse.

The read path.

A companion study establishes a three-condition execution contract under which file-backed weights reach accelerator-class bandwidth without an intermediate framework-owned copy: adopt the mapping inside the framework execution path, keep activations accelerator-resident, and order work on the accelerator queue (Si et al., 2026). Under this contract, the GPU reads a page-cache-resident expert at the same bandwidth as a framework-owned allocation, so residency policy determines performance once the copy path has been removed. We use the execution contract from that study and re-measure every bandwidth constant on the evaluation node: 2938 GB/s for HBM weight reads; 327 GB/s for GPU reads from file-backed host pages; 330 GB/s for framework-owned hostAlloc storage; 23 GB/s for unregistered malloc storage; 27.0 GB/s for NVMe; and 346 GB/s for overlapped copy-then-compute streaming over a link with a 368.5 GB/s ceiling. A second independent run reproduces each rate within 0.8% (computed on unrounded rates). This paper evaluates which file-backed pages should remain resident and whether eviction should be managed by the kernel or by a user-space expert cache.

3. Router Locality at Three Scales

Frequency-based pinning assumes that a sufficiently concentrated and stable set of experts can be identified in advance. We test this assumption using per-layer top-kk router selections from four workload domains—systems prose, code generation, mathematics, and travel planning (labeled chat in the figures and tables)—on the three models in §2 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Qwen Team, 2025; Kimi Team, 2026). The production-model traces come from its serving engine (242–290 engine iterations, 299 accepted tokens per domain); Qwen3-30B-A3B and 671B DeepSeek-V3 are traced through an evaluation callback added to llama.cpp (Gerganov and contributors, 2023) (400 and 300 steps per domain, plus 4,000-step Qwen3-30B-A3B runs for coverage asymptotics). Prefill records are excluded throughout (§2).

Fact 1: concentration decreases with expert count.

Rank–frequency slopes are Zipf-like in all three models: α\alpha is 1.10–1.26 at E=128E{=}128 and near or below 1 at the larger pools (0.86–0.93 at E=256E{=}256, 1.00–1.04 at E=896E{=}896). At trillion scale, the top-8 experts per layer carry only 13–16% of selections, compared with 34–42% at E=128E{=}128.

Fact 2: concentration varies sharply across layers.

In the production model, the first routed layer assigns only 3.9% of its selections to the top eight experts, the most concentrated layer reaches 18.0%, a 4.6×\times spread, and the final layer sits at 10.7%. Per-layer union coverage varies from 890 of 896 experts at the widest layer to 646 at the narrowest, with early layers covering more of the pool than the deepest quarter. DeepSeek-V3 shows a similar profile. The widest layers demand the most cache capacity, and a global LRU pool adapts its allocation to this per-layer variation, whereas a static per-layer quota must be tuned for each model.

Fact 3: at E=128E{=}128, concentration increases in long contexts.

In the 4,000-step Qwen3-30B-A3B runs, the fitted slope rises to 1.54–1.71, and 64-token reuse rises from 95–96% (Table 1) to about 99%. The longer traces are therefore at least as cacheable as the shorter ones.

Fact 4: recency is strong at every scale.

At W1W_{1}, 32–36% of the production model’s selections repeat the previous token’s experts, rising to 80–82% within 64 tokens. Most of that reuse is already present at W8W_{8} (57–59%), so a modest cache captures much of the available recency.

Fact 5: static hot sets do not transfer across domains.

The top expert sets of different domains overlap by as little as 0.066 (Jaccard) in Qwen3-30B-A3B and at most 0.188 in the production model (Table 1). A pin set learned on one workload therefore has limited overlap with the hot set of another. Facts 1–4 show substantial locality, but that locality is expressed more reliably through recent reuse than through a fixed global ranking.

Fact 6: coverage continues to grow without saturating.

Within 300 steps, every domain touches 64–69% of the production pool. The 4,000-step Qwen3-30B-A3B runs show the longer trend: coverage reaches 73–81% and continues to increase at 4,000 steps, while each additional step reuses recently selected experts at approximately 99%. Because coverage does not saturate, no fixed subset of the pool suffices: dropping experts changes the executed model, whereas caching preserves the full pool and pays the measured miss latency instead (§4).

At the smallest budgets, recency thrashes.

Fig. 1 evaluates static frequency pinning, LFU, LRU, and Belady’s offline optimum under identical windows: every policy warms on the first 60% of iterations and is scored on the final 40%. Comparing a warm frequency table against cold-start LRU produces an artifactual crossover that disappears once both policies use the same warm-up and scoring windows; the small-budget inversion below survives fair windows. At the smallest simulated budget (B=8B{=}8, at or below the routed fan-out kk), LRU evicts entries before their next reuse. At B=8B{=}8 with k=16k{=}16, it hits 0.5% while LFU reaches 12.7% and static frequency 9.8%. Frequency therefore performs best in this tiny-cache regime, and the same inversion appears at E=128E{=}128 (LRU 30.1% versus LFU 36.0% and static 33.9%).

At host-tier budgets, recency wins and remains ahead.

From B=32B{=}32 upward—approximately 52 GB at production scale, just below the smallest measured capacity (C=64C{=}64 GB; Table 2)—the ranking reverses and remains stable. At E=128E{=}128, the two policies fall within the domain spread (75% LRU versus 73% static at B=32B{=}32). At E=256E{=}256, LRU leads at every simulated budget, including B=8B{=}8, and reaches 48% versus 35% at B=32B{=}32; at E=896E{=}896 it leads from B=16B{=}16 upward in the per-layer regime (19.4% versus 15.5% on the chat domain at B=16B{=}16, and 44% versus 23% at B=32B{=}32). At trillion scale, LRU captures approximately 70% of Belady’s optimum (44 of 62%), whereas static frequency captures roughly one third (23 of 62%). As the expert head becomes less concentrated and the hot set shifts across domains, a static ranking becomes stale while recency adapts.

Bounds in the policy comparison.

In Fig. 1, the Belady bound falls as EE grows—larger expert pools are intrinsically harder to cache—and the LRU-to-Belady gap widens with EE. The miss-reduction potential available to predictive advice (§7) therefore grows with the expert pool, whereas a static rank list does not close the gap.

Global-pool and per-layer results agree on these traces.

A page cache is one pool keyed by (layer, expert), rather than 92 fixed per-layer caches. Layered-paging theory shows that fixed per-layer allocations can have an unbounded competitive ratio in the worst case (Angelopoulos et al., 2025). We therefore simulate both allocation regimes on the production model’s prose trace and its evaluation window: one global budget of NN experts shared across layers and the equal-split per-layer budget used above. On that trace, we do not observe the worst-case separation: global and equal-split LRU remain within 2.7 pp at every budget, and the policy ordering is identical in both regimes at every budget from B=32B{=}32 upward. At the 1,472-expert budget (B=16B{=}16) the two regimes disagree on LRU versus static (16.8% versus 18.8% global, 19.5% versus 17.5% per-layer). The global pool also allocates fewer distinct experts to the more concentrated layers without model-specific quotas.

Batching increases simulated misses.

Merging the four domain traces iteration-by-iteration through the canonical parser preserves every speculative and fallback pass; the union is truncated to the 242 iterations of the shortest trace, which places 1078 of the 4×2994\times 299{} accepted tokens inside the merged window. The batch-4 union transfers 108 GB per step, corresponding to only 1.08×\times deduplication. Four streams sharing one budget lose hit rate under the same 60/40 window: at a 25%-of-pool budget, the rate falls from 78% for one stream to 64% for batch 4. The resulting rise in misses is well below the 4×4\times demand of four independent streams, but still yields a simulated per-token miss ratio of 1.45×\times at a fixed ≈200{\approx}200 GB budget (B=125B{=}125 per layer); the corresponding ratio for Qwen3-30B-A3B is 1.54×\times at B=32B{=}32, ≈4.4{\approx}4.4 GB.

4. Iteration Time and Device Traffic versus DRAM Capacity

We measure iteration time and block-layer device traffic across DRAM capacities under three capacity mechanisms. Iteration time varies smoothly with capacity under every mechanism; one reclaim configuration additionally inflates device traffic above the simulated miss demand, and §5 analyzes it separately.

Method.

We replay the production model’s prose trace against the full 1.45 TB pool on a GH200 node (NVIDIA Corporation, 2023) (480 GB Grace DRAM, 3.9 TB NVMe; machine A), through a native harness that reads exactly the experts selected by each recorded router pass. A second GH200 node of the same memory configuration but with an NVMe class approximately 3×\times faster (machine B) is used for the mechanism cross-validation below and for the equal-memory, prefetch, and end-to-end experiments of §§6–9. The canonical parser yields 285 iterations and 299 accepted tokens, with speculative and fallback passes replayed as issued. For the principal sweep, capacity CC is set by an mlocked balloon (Waldspurger, 2002). For each capacity point, we drop caches, verify the locked size, run one warm-up replay, and measure a second. The sweep is repeated three times in randomized capacity order. Every pass snapshots /proc/diskstats, /proc/vmstat, and pressure-stall accounting, so device bytes are measured at the block layer.

Cells enforced with the cgroup wall follow Algorithm 1: warm-up and measurement execute in one accounting scope. With separate scopes, file pages from the terminated warm-up scope are reparented without being charged to the measured scope, and a nominal C=256C{=}256 GB measurement reproduces the 448 GB point; the per-run memory.current timeline exposes the miscount.

The observed curve.

Median iteration time increases smoothly and monotonically from 0.99 s at C=448C{=}448 GB to 2.76 s at 64 GB, with run-to-run spread of 0.5–4.0% (Table 2). The curve covers one trace, one host, four capacities, and one kernel version. Selected capacities are remeasured with one mechanism changed at a time in §§5–6, and §8 sizes a deployment from it.

An inverse-capacity reference for device bytes.

Measured device traffic follows an inverse-capacity reference anchored at the 448 GB point (Fig. 2, right): halving the cache approximately doubles NVMe traffic, from 5.3 to 33.6 GB per iteration, with per-point deviations between -9.7% and +5.0% (Table 2). The reference has no fitted parameter beyond its anchor.

A constant-free demand diagnostic.

The demand model does not estimate elapsed time. Raw-device probes read 27.0 GB/s cold and 61.4 GB/s warm, while the replay path’s effective rate is 29.6 GB/s—a spread of more than 2×\times—so a time model calibrated from any single bandwidth constant would not transfer reliably across systems. Instead, we simulate LRU at capacity CC, multiply misses by expert size, and compare the result with measured device bytes (Table 2). A ratio above one indicates re-read amplification; it rises from 0.99×\times at 448 GB to 2.22×\times at C=64C{=}64 GB. This diagnostic identifies excess I/O without assigning a machine-specific time constant.

Agreement across capacity mechanisms.

Ballooning reserves anonymous memory and treats the remainder as the capacity available to the file tier. We therefore cross-validate selected points under a cgroup-v2 MemoryMax wall (Algorithm 1) and under mem= boots, in which the kernel cannot use the omitted DRAM. When reclaim policy is held constant, the mechanisms agree in median iteration time within 5.1% at the hit-dominated end (balloon versus cgroup wall at C=448C{=}448 GB, across the two machines) and within 14.9% in the deepest matched cell (C=64C{=}64 GB with MGLRU off, machine A balloon versus machine B cgroup wall). A mem= boot at an effective capacity of 339 GB differs by 0.5% from the balloon curve interpolated to that capacity (Fig. 3, right). One further cross-machine pair differs by more than these figures because the two machines’ storage devices differ in bandwidth by approximately 3×\times; it is excluded from the agreement numbers. Nominal CC is therefore used as the effective cache capacity.

Batched capacity.

We replay the canonical batch-4 union plan from §3, preserving all speculative and fallback passes and accounting for 1078 accepted tokens. Per-accepted-token time is 0.82 s at C=448C{=}448 GB and 1.30 s at 256 GB, against 0.94 and 1.31 s for the single-stream replay at the same capacities (-13% and 0%). The batch-4 replay’s per-iteration spread is also narrower than the single-stream spread at the same capacity, consistent with the union of four router streams smoothing aggregate miss demand.

Darwin response.

An M-series Mac (128 GB, Darwin, 16 KB pages) replaying Qwen3-30B-A3B also exhibits a smooth response, from 20.6 ms per step with the 17.6 GB pool fully cached to 26.3 ms at a 9 GB file cache. Ballooning that leaves the desktop responsive cannot reach the lowest-capacity Darwin regime, so the reclaim attribution in §5 is limited to Linux. On Darwin, the compressor absorbs balloon pressure before the file cache yields, and Metal-wired pages are not evictable.

5. Low-Capacity Amplification Depends on Reclaim Configuration

From C=256C{=}256 GB downward, the device traffic measured with the balloon rises above the traffic predicted from misses (1.22×\times at 256 GB, 1.50×\times at 128 GB, 2.22×\times at 64 GB; Table 2). At C=64C{=}64 GB the tier reads 33.6 GB per iteration against a nominal miss demand of 15.1 GB, which implies that some pages are evicted and read again within an iteration. Toggling the reclaim implementation isolates one contributing condition. In a separate three-run reclaim toggle on the same machine (distinct from the capacity sweep of Table 2, whose median for this cell is 33.6 GB), MGLRU—the default in the tested configuration—produces 36 GB per iteration (31.1–50.9 across runs), with kswapd scanning 5.5–6.9 pages per page reclaimed. Classic LRU produces 14 GB per iteration (13.8–19.0), with a scan-to-steal ratio of 1.0 (Fig. 3, left). MGLRU is therefore necessary but not sufficient for the amplification; the next comparison varies the capacity mechanism as well.

Amplification requires two conditions.

We repeat the deep-pressure experiment on a second machine under all three capacity mechanisms—the cgroup wall and the balloon at C=64C{=}64 GB, and mem= at the lowest boot that leaves the system stable (102 GB visible, effective capacity ≈93{\approx}93 GB)—and toggle MGLRU within each condition (Fig. 3, middle). Under the cgroup MemoryMax wall at C=64C{=}64 GB, traffic is effectively unchanged between MGLRU enabled and disabled (16.5 and 16.5 GB per iteration). Under the physical mem= boot, MGLRU is also near nominal and slightly lower than classic LRU (16.4 versus 18.1 GB). Under the balloon at C=64C{=}64 GB, the same capacity as the cgroup wall, amplification returns: 33.6 GB with MGLRU and a scan-to-steal ratio of 2.4, compared with 16.8 GB after disabling MGLRU. Machine A’s reclaim toggle, on a device approximately 3×\times slower, records 36 GB in the corresponding cell. The combined evidence attributes amplification to the interaction between MGLRU and balloon pressure created by a very large mlocked anonymous region. In the affected cell, 81% of memory is locked.

Dependence on the locked fraction.

Reducing the locked fraction to 74% in the C≈93C{\approx}93 GB balloon condition removes the amplification on machine B: MGLRU then produces 18.5 GB per iteration, compared with 23.7 GB under classic LRU. Within the balloon condition, amplification is therefore present at 81% locked (C=64C{=}64 GB) and absent at 74% locked (C≈93C{\approx}93 GB). A balloon sets the locked fraction and the remaining capacity with one knob, so this pair does not separate the two variables by itself; the separation comes from the non-balloon cells, which show no amplification at either capacity. Classic LRU under the balloon remains close to nominal in the median but has a wider run-to-run range on machine A (13.8–19.0 GB) than that of the cgroup-wall repetitions, which differ by at most 0.1 GB. Ballooning is therefore a less stable capacity-control mechanism even when it does not cause amplification.

Methodological consequence.

Ballooning is widely used to emulate smaller-memory machines (Waldspurger, 2002), and the principal capacity sweep uses balloons with the tested kernel default, so its lowest-capacity points include the additional traffic produced by the combination of MGLRU and a high locked fraction. The overstatement is approximately 2×\times: 2.0×\times relative to the cgroup wall at matched capacity on machine B, and 2.6×\times between MGLRU enabled and disabled on machine A. At an effective capacity of approximately 93 GB, the physical-memory condition records 16.4 GB per iteration under mem=, whereas interpolation from the balloon-conditioned curve implies approximately 24 GB. Table 2 therefore labels the rows below 448 GB balloon-conditioned, and physical-memory reductions are sized from the mem= points. Capacity studies that use ballooning should cross-check at least one low-capacity point with a cgroup limit or a mem= boot. A generation-counter analysis of how MGLRU ages pages behind a large unevictable region remains future work (Zhao, 2022).

Operator guidance.

Production systems can create a similar condition when large arenas are mlocked for pinned expert tiers, HBM staging pools, or other reservations. On hosts with a large unevictable fraction, operators can compare kswapd scan-to-steal ratios with 1.0 and block-device bytes with nominal miss demand. In our measurements, a scan-to-steal ratio above 2 appears in every cell in which amplification exceeds 2×\times and in no reclaim-neutral cell; this is an empirical indicator for the tested systems, not a general threshold. The experiments support three mitigations: confining the streaming reader in a memory-limited cgroup, reducing the locked region, or benchmarking with MGLRU disabled. The last change reduces traffic by a factor of 2.6 in the affected condition. Pressure-stall accounting (Weiner et al., 2022) provides an additional operational signal.

6. Pinned Arena versus Page Cache at Equal Memory

User-space expert caches commonly pin frequently selected experts. We evaluate the mechanism and policy separately: whether serving a hit from an mlocked arena is faster than serving it from the page cache, and whether a static frequency table retains better bytes than kernel recency. The comparison enforces equal memory for every run.

Setup.

All configurations use the same native harness, thread pool, and destination buffers, and perform one copy per access; only the source of bytes on a hit differs. The pinned configuration preloads the most frequent experts into one mlocked arena. Its frequency table is computed from the evaluated trace, so it is an oracle upper bound rather than a deployable policy. Misses read from the full pool. The page-cache configuration receives the same budget, held entirely as file cache and with no policy tuning, and the hybrid configuration divides the budget between an arena and the page cache. Equal memory is enforced with the cgroup protocol in Algorithm 1. At 256 GB, retained pinned runs record VmLck=238 GiB and 256 GB of one-time preload traffic outside the measured interval, and every retained run reaches its peak memory.current at the wall with no OOM event. We run two interleaved repetitions per point in randomized order.

Mechanism overhead.

At C=256C{=}256 GB, the oracle-pinned arena completes an iteration in 1.04 s, compared with 1.13 s for the page cache, a 1.09×\times difference (1.11×\times at 128 GB; Fig. 4). Both configurations read nearly the same amount from storage, 7.4 and 7.2 GB per iteration; the device counters therefore rule out byte selection as the cause, and the timing difference reflects the page-cache hit path—lookup and mapping on hits, plus reclaim work at the memory wall. Disabling readahead with POSIX_FADV_RANDOM increases the page-cache time to 1.80 s, so readahead is not the source of the gap. The gap is specific to this pread-based replay. Under the zero-copy execution contract (Si et al., 2026), the GPU reads resident file-backed and framework-owned pages at 327 and 330 GB/s (§2), so the corresponding overhead there should be smaller than 1.09×\times; that path is not timed per token in this study. A 50/50 hybrid split at C=256C{=}256 GB takes 1.11 s, between the two pure configurations.

Placement policy.

We compare the fraction of total demand served without device access. At C=256C{=}256 GB the page cache serves 75.3% and the oracle-pinned arena, on its own domain, 74.6% (73.2% from arena hits plus 1.4 points from misses served out of the ≈6{\approx}6 GiB of scope headroom above the arena; Algorithm 1); at C=128C{=}128 GB the figures are 55.4% and 57.0%. At equal capacity, kernel recency therefore serves demand within about 1.6 points of an oracle frequency table on the domain from which that table was computed. (The arena’s table is built from the whole replayed trace; the fair-window table below is trained on the first 60% only, hence its lower same-domain figure.) Under domain shift the table degrades: in the fair-window simulation of Fig. 5 (B=159B{=}159 experts per layer, ≈256{\approx}256 GB), the prose-trained table reaches 57% on its own domain against LRU’s 74%, and falls to 21–45% off domain while table-free LRU holds 70–71%. The trace analysis in §3 attributes this difference to cross-domain changes in expert selection, with Jaccard similarity as low as 0.101.

7. The Router as a Prefetch Advisor

Once layer ℓ\ell has routed, a predictor can estimate the experts that layer ℓ+1\ell{+}1 will require before their reads begin. We measure both the quality of this information and the interface used to deliver it. Prediction quality and replay use one recorded expert-set plan: the production engine writes it, and the replay reads it unchanged. The oracle next-pass plan provides a one-layer upper bound. Both plans use the same bounded worker with one thread and one overwritable slot. The worker either submits posix_fadvise(WILLNEED) or performs a blocking pread, and it counts submitted, overwritten, and completed hints in every condition.

Measured prediction quality.

The production engine’s one-layer lookahead predictor (PILOT) caches next-layer gate weights and recalls 64.7% of decode-time selections, with a per-layer range of 1–84%. Recall varies substantially across layers, indicating that a uniform prefetch policy spends effort on layers with limited predictability. Previous-token recurrence, which is available without model-specific lookahead, is 32–36%; the learned predictor approximately doubles this baseline.

Delivery interface.

At C=256C{=}256 GB under the cgroup wall, oracle advice changes median iteration time from 1.134 to 1.077 s, an improvement of 5.0%; the oracle plan covers the full next pass and submits 27,407 hints, none overwritten. The measured PILOT plan submits 5,278 hints, none overwritten, and yields 1.131 s, a 0.3% change at 64.7% recall—the same magnitude as the ≈0.3{\approx}0.3% two-run spread. The oracle and PILOT plans differ in hint volume as well as recall, so their gap reflects both prediction quality and the number of experts each plan covers. Delivering the same plans through blocking reads yields 1.151 s for the oracle and 1.153 s for PILOT, 1.5% and 1.7% slower than no prefetch (Fig. 6): a single bounded blocking worker does not keep ahead of the eight-thread demand stream, and most of its reads are overwritten in the slot before completion (17,553 of 27,407 for the oracle plan). The advisory interface issues readahead without delaying demand and discards stale work when the slot is overwritten.

Lookahead depth and targeting.

One layer provides a natural horizon because the transfer can overlap with computation in the current layer. Deeper prediction compounds errors across layers and reduces the probability that prefetched experts are used. The observed per-layer recall range motivates suppressing hints for poorly predicted layers. Such targeting is possible because, under advisory delivery, an incorrect or late hint costs transfer efficiency without changing the executed experts. Belady’s 62% hit rate compared with LRU’s 44% at B=32B{=}32 shows that better future information could eliminate approximately one third of the remaining LRU misses.

8. Placement Rules and the Serving Procedure

The capacity response in §4 characterizes the DRAM tier. A complete serving node also includes accelerator memory and storage. Combining the bandwidth constants re-measured on the evaluation node (§2) with that capacity response yields three placement rules and, with them, the serving procedure of Algorithm 2.

Rule 1: admit demand-read pages to DRAM

A miss already incurs the NVMe read, and allowing the resulting file pages to remain in the page cache adds no I/O to that miss. The remaining risk is that admitted pages displace a more valuable working set; Algorithm 2 removes that risk directly by keeping the dense spine accelerator-resident or separately locked. Retaining demand-read expert pages then preserves the possibility of future hits and yields the 5.3×\times repeated-read improvement measured in §9.

Rule 2: promote high-reuse experts to HBM

Promoting an expert of SS bytes to HBM costs one overlapped transfer S/346S/346 and saves S⁡(1/327−1/2938)S(1/327-1/2938) on each subsequent use, with the rates in GB/s. The breakeven reuse count is

r∗=1/3461/327−1/2938= 1.06.r^{\ast}\;=\;\frac{1/346}{1/327-1/2938}\;=\;1.06.

On the measured coherent link, the first reuse repays the transfer. HBM allocation can therefore prioritize experts with the highest expected reuse until capacity is exhausted.

Rule 3: prefer direct file-backed reads when adoption and streaming have similar rates.

Direct GPU reads from file-backed host memory are within 5.6% of overlapped streaming on the measured node (computed on unrounded rates). In this range, file-backed adoption avoids the copy engine, staging buffers, and double-buffering required by explicit streaming.

Dependence on memory topology.

The relative value of these rules changes with the accelerator-memory topology (Si et al., 2026). On unified-memory systems, adopted file-backed pages and framework-owned allocations occupy the same physical memory domain, so host capacity and reclaim policy dominate. On discrete PCIe systems, unregistered host reads are limited to the 23 GB/s regime in our measurements, making HBM ownership or explicit streaming necessary for high bandwidth. Coherent-link systems such as the measured GH200 support all three paths: file-backed host reads, HBM promotion, and streaming. The kernel-owned DRAM tier is therefore most directly useful on unified- and coherent-memory systems; on PCIe systems, it remains a storage tier below an HBM-resident working set.

Worked sizing example.

The same measurements support capacity planning in the style of the five-minute rule (Gray and Putzolu, 1987). For a target maximum iteration time of two seconds, Fig. 2 indicates approximately 128 GB of DRAM, where the measured median is 1.95 s and device traffic is 17.4 GB per iteration. A 256 GB allocation yields 1.37 s at 9.8 GB. These rows are balloon-conditioned (§5); treat the 128 GB figure as an upper bound on the DRAM the target requires. At C=448C{=}448 GB, the replay sustains 1.01 engine iterations per second per stream, and the batch-4 replay requires 0.82 s per accepted token; compute is excluded from these figures. The estimates apply to the measured replay, subject to the reclaim conditions of §5 and the batching behavior of §4.

9. End-to-End Validation in the Production Engine

Algorithm 2 requires no kernel modification. We evaluate its admission steps in the production engine: first in the existing reader, then along the complete decode path.

Cache-admission microbenchmark.

We use the production engine’s existing pread reader, including its threads, buffers, and files, to repeat reads of an 11.2 GB expert set. Under the shipped F_NOCACHE policy, every pass incurs device traffic and reaches 13.1 GB/s. Enabling cache admission raises throughput to 68.9 GB/s, a 5.3×\times improvement under the same reader and engine.

End-to-end validation.

We run full decode through the production engine on the GH200 with three measured pairs per prompt, ordered admission-first, F_NOCACHE-first, and by a seeded shuffle. A run is retained only if the engine reports the expected CUDA MoE backend and produces a non-degenerate output. At ample capacity—no capacity mechanism applied, on the full 480 GB host—enabling admission improves median steady-decode time by 1.09–1.10×\times per prompt (Table 3). Total time, which includes the policy-independent cold model load, improves by 1.03–1.04×\times. The two runs in each pair produce identical 60-token ID sequences and the same SHA-256 output hash. Table 3 reports the median and per-prompt range across the three pairs per prompt. These runs are single-stream; §4 reports the batch-4 union replay.

Cross-process sharing.

The page cache is system-wide, so processes share one physical copy, benefit from pages loaded by another process, and retain cached pages across process restarts (Si et al., 2026). A conventional user-space arena is private to each process, which can require nn copies of the hot set for nn serving processes.

Validation scope.

The end-to-end validation uses one production engine. On the 480 GB host, the available open model (17.6 GB of experts in an 18.6 GB file) does not exercise this tier: llama.cpp’s --cpu-moe places experts in anonymous memory and bypasses the page cache, while without that option the model fits in HBM. A separate Apple-silicon experiment measures decode time under mmap-based and buffered loading of the same model and finds the two within 2%.

10. Limitations

Replay scope.

The capacity, policy, and prefetch campaigns replay recorded router passes through the expert I/O tier with compute excluded. The end-to-end measurements in §9 evaluate how this tier composes with a production engine at ample capacity. The replay results therefore characterize I/O-tier behavior and provide bounds for, rather than complete measurements of, deployed serving.

Oracle upper bound.

The pinned arena’s frequency table is computed from the evaluated trace. This gives the arena information that a deployed system would not possess and biases the comparison in its favor. The off-domain experiment in Fig. 5 directly measures the sensitivity of the static table to workload change.

Scope of the reclaim attribution.

The reclaim experiments cover two machines, Linux 6.8, and one NVMe device class per machine. The attribution to the interaction between MGLRU and high-locked-fraction balloon pressure is behavioral: it rests on same-machine comparisons across three capacity mechanisms and two locked fractions on machine B, with the balloon reclaim toggle reproduced independently on machine A and the MGLRU state recorded for every run. A generation-counter analysis explaining how pages age behind the large unevictable region remains future work. Balloon traffic is also unstable from run to run in both reclaim conditions: with MGLRU enabled it spans 31.1–50.9 GB per iteration across repetitions, and with MGLRU disabled 13.8–19.0 GB, a 38% range, so the disabled condition is close to nominal but retains measurable variability. Darwin reproduces smooth capacity degradation but cannot safely reach the corresponding lowest-capacity regime.

Traces.

Production-model traces contain 242–290 engine iterations and 299 accepted tokens per domain, with speculative and fallback passes replayed as issued. Four prompt families represent the workload domains. The 4,000-step asymptotic experiment uses the 128-expert model, so longer traces from the production model remain future work. Greedy decoding makes the recorded access streams reproducible; the results do not establish behavior under stochastic sampling. Cross-domain results are reported as observed ranges across the four workloads.

Correctness invariance.

Under greedy decoding, the recorded expert selections are the exact access stream issued by the engine and are replayed in their original order; residency policy changes only where the selected bytes are served from (§9 reports the paired output hashes).

Scope exclusions.

Multi-node serving, quality effects of pruning instead of caching, and request-arrival processes are outside the measurement scope. Each adds a system or modeling dimension beyond the single-node residency tier characterized here.

Reproducibility.

The replay harness, simulators, and analysis pipeline will be submitted for artifact evaluation.

11. Related Work

Mixture-of-experts models.

Sparse expert layers (Shazeer et al., 2017) scaled through GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2021), Switch (Fedus et al., 2022), and GLaM (Du et al., 2022) to open models including Mixtral (Jiang et al., 2024), Qwen3-30B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2025), DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), and the Kimi K2/K3 line (Kimi Team, 2025; Kimi Team, 2026). These models increase total expert capacity while activating only a subset per token. The trace study in §3 examines how increasing expert count changes the relative performance of frequency and recency policies.

MoE offload and expert caching.

MoE-Infinity (Xue et al., 2025) uses observed routing behavior to prefetch and cache experts in user space. PowerInfer (Song et al., 2024) places frequently activated neurons on the GPU using offline profiles. LLM in a Flash (Alizadeh et al., 2024) reduces flash traffic through activation windowing and increases transfer granularity through row-column bundling. DeepSpeed-MoE (Rajbhandari et al., 2022) develops system and model optimizations for large-scale MoE inference. Mixtral-offloading uses an expert LRU (Eliseev and Mazur, 2023); SiDA-MoE (Du et al., 2024) predicts expert activation offline with a hash-based sparsity model to place experts between GPU and host memory; Pre-gated MoE (Hwang et al., 2024) moves gating ahead of expert transfer; Fiddler (Kamahori et al., 2025) coordinates CPU and GPU expert execution; and EdgeMoE (Yi et al., 2025) targets sparse-model inference on mobile devices. FlexGen (Sheng et al., 2023) schedules dense-model offload and addresses a complementary problem.

FineMoE uses fine-grained expert-selection patterns and prompt-semantic hints to guide prefetching, caching, and offloading (Yu et al., 2026). SpecPrefetch uses a lightweight predictor only to initiate asynchronous transfer, while the native router determines the experts that execute (Kong et al., 2026); this separation corresponds to the advisory interface evaluated in §7. Angelopoulos et al. formulate expert caching as a layered paging problem, show that fixed per-layer cache allocations can have an unbounded competitive ratio, and propose a layer-aware extension of LRU (Angelopoulos et al., 2025). Motivated by that result, we compare equal per-layer allocation with one global capacity pool in §3 and find a difference of at most 2.7 pp on the production prose trace.

Kernel-owned expert tier.

Prior expert-offload systems primarily manage residency in user space, with different expert granularities, prediction sources, and transfer mechanisms. This paper adds an equal-memory page-cache baseline (§6), measures the reclaim behavior inherited from the operating system (§§4–5), and identifies page-granular sharing across processes as a property a per-process arena cannot provide (§9). A companion study establishes the zero-copy execution contract used for the reads themselves (Si et al., 2026) (§2); the present paper evaluates residency management for the pages being read.

LLM serving systems.

PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) applies paging to the KV cache in user space, and Orca (Yu et al., 2022) introduces iteration-level continuous batching. Both concern activation memory and scheduling and can be combined with a kernel-managed weight tier. llama.cpp (Gerganov and contributors, 2023) uses mmap-based model loading by default; this paper characterizes the capacity and workload conditions under which that approach is effective for expert weights.

OS memory management.

Ballooning as a capacity-control mechanism descends from VMware ESX (Waldspurger, 2002). TMO uses pressure-stall accounting to manage datacenter memory offload (Weiner et al., 2022), and TPP places pages across CXL memory tiers (Maruf et al., 2023). The capacity-response curve in §4 describes the expert-tier demand that such controllers would need to satisfy. MGLRU (Zhao, 2022) is the reclaim implementation evaluated in §5. Database systems have documented limitations of mmap-based buffer management (Crotty et al., 2022). The evaluated expert pool is read-only, sequential within each expert, and shareable across processes, unlike the mutable transactional workloads those limitations concern.

Caching theory.

Prior caching work spans Belady’s optimal replacement (Belady, 1966), working sets (Denning, 1968), and policies combining recency and frequency, such as ARC (Megiddo and Modha, 2003). The trace experiments compare recency, frequency, and Belady’s optimum on MoE routing traces (§3). The five-minute rule (Gray and Putzolu, 1987) motivates the reuse-based placement calculation in §8. Work on caching with machine-learned advice (Lykouris and Vassilvitskii, 2018; Rohatgi, 2020; Antoniadis et al., 2020) bounds the value of predictions; §7 measures how much of that bound a one-layer predictor realizes through advisory and blocking interfaces.

12. Conclusion

A 1.45 TB MoE model cannot hold its expert pool in DRAM, so the serving system must manage partial residency. In the measured workloads, a same-domain oracle frequency table at best matches recency, and its hit rate degrades under domain shift. At equal enforced memory, an oracle-pinned arena retains a 1.09–1.11×\times timing advantage over the page cache in the pread-based replay. Because device traffic is nearly equal in both configurations, that cost lies in the page-cache lookup and reclaim path, not in which bytes each policy keeps. Across the evaluated capacity and workload regimes, the kernel tier remains close to the oracle baseline while requiring no workload-specific frequency table, adapting to domain changes, and sharing pages across processes. Router information is still useful for admission, HBM promotion, and nonblocking predictive advice, while general eviction stays with the kernel. Two system effects require explicit control: MGLRU can amplify traffic when most memory is unevictable, and balloon-based capacity experiments on the tested configuration can overstate low-capacity device traffic by approximately 2×\times. Reliable evaluation therefore requires enforced capacity, per-run accounting checks, and block-layer measurement of device traffic.
